Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.

We represent: habeas petitioner.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that counsel is ineffective under Strickland for failing to investigate and present available mitigating evidence at a capital sentencing.

Cite at least six decisions of the Ninth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### Trial counsel rendered ineffective assistance at the penalty phase by failing to investigate and present readily available mitigating evidence.

#### A. Counsel's performance was deficient.

To prevail, Petitioner must show deficient performance and resulting prejudice. *Strickland v. Washington*, 466 U.S. 668, 687-88, 694 (1984). Counsel has "a duty to make reasonable investigations or to make a reasonable decision that makes particular investigations unnecessary." *Id.* at 691. In capital sentencing, that duty includes a thorough investigation of the defendant's background. *Wiggins v. Smith*, 539 U.S. 510, 522-25 (2003); *Williams v. Taylor*, 529 U.S. 362, 395-96 (2000). Strategic choices made after less than complete investigation are reasonable only to the extent that reasonable professional judgment supports the limits on investigation. *Wiggins*, 539 U.S. at 533. A decision not to pursue mitigation cannot be called "strategic" when it rests on counsel's own failure to learn what was available. *Id.* at 526-28.

This Court has repeatedly granted relief where counsel abdicated that duty. In *Correll v. Ryan*, 539 F.3d 938, 942-52 (9th Cir. 2008), counsel's cursory investigation missed evidence of the defendant's mental impairments and troubled history, and the court held that omission was not a reasonable strategic choice. In *Lambright v. Schriro*, 490 F.3d 1103, 1116-20 (9th Cir. 2007), counsel began preparing late, did little to explore the defendant's background, and never pursued obvious leads. The court held that performance deficient. *See also Stankewitz v. Woodford*, 365 F.3d 706, 719-22 (9th Cir. 2004) (failure to investigate and present available social-history and mental-health mitigation); *Douglas v. Woodford*, 316 F.3d 1079, 1085-88 (9th Cir. 2003) (failure to investigate and present mitigating evidence was deficient performance and not tactical); *Caro v. Calderon*, 165 F.3d 1223, 1226-27 (9th Cir. 1999) (failure to investigate and present evidence of toxic-chemical exposure and resulting impairment).

Here, counsel [describe: hours spent, records not requested, family and witnesses not interviewed, experts not retained]. Records and witnesses that would have revealed [abuse, deprivation, cognitive impairment, mental illness] were available and, in some instances, were identified in materials counsel already possessed. As in *Wiggins*, *Correll*, and *Lambright*, those leads would have led a reasonable attorney to investigate further. *See Rompilla v. Beard*, 545 U.S. 374, 387-90 (2005). Counsel's failure to do so reflected inattention, not strategy.

#### B. The omitted evidence creates a reasonable probability of a different sentence.

Prejudice exists if there is a reasonable probability that, absent counsel's errors, at least one juror would have voted against death. *Strickland*, 466 U.S. at 695; *Wiggins*, 539 U.S. at 537. The court must reweigh the aggravating evidence against the totality of available mitigation, including what could have been presented. *Williams*, 529 U.S. at 397-98; *Porter v. McCollum*, 558 U.S. 30, 41-44 (2009) (per curiam). Petitioner need not show that the mitigation would have outweighed the aggravation as a certainty, only that confidence in the outcome is undermined. *Strickland*, 466 U.S. at 694.

This Court has found prejudice where the jury heard little or nothing about the defendant's history and impairments. *Correll*, 539 F.3d at 951-52; *Lambright*, 490 F.3d at 1121-25; *Stankewitz*, 365 F.3d at 722-24; *Douglas*, 316 F.3d at 1090-91; *see also Earp v. Ornoski*, 431 F.3d 1158, 1173-76 (9th Cir. 2005) (counsel's failure to investigate and present available mitigation at capital sentencing); *Jennings v. Woodford*, 290 F.3d 1006, 1014-19 (9th Cir. 2002) (same). The jury here heard a one-dimensional account of Petitioner. The omitted evidence would have supplied a human context for the offense, explained Petitioner's impairments, and given jurors a principled reason to choose life. Mitigating evidence of this kind bears directly on moral culpability, which is the central question at capital sentencing. *Wiggins*, 539 U.S. at 535; *Porter*, 558 U.S. at 41-43. Against the aggravating evidence, [summarize aggravators and their strength], there is a reasonable probability that at least one juror would have voted for life.

#### C. The state court's contrary decision is unreasonable under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d).

To the extent the state court rejected this claim on the merits, its decision unreasonably applied *Strickland* and *Wiggins*. 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(1); *Williams*, 529 U.S. at 405-06. It credited counsel's supposed strategy without asking whether the investigation behind it was reasonable, and it assessed prejudice without reweighing the omitted evidence against the aggravation. *See Porter*, 558 U.S. at 39-42; *Sears v. Upton*, 561 U.S. 945, 954-56 (2010) (per curiam). The decision rested on an unreasonable view of the record. *See* 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(2). Alternatively, if the Court reaches the claim de novo, relief is warranted for the reasons above.
